newsitem.title: USA: US, Japan car trade tensions seen rising with dlr.
newsitem.headline: US, Japan car trade tensions seen rising with dlr.

text.p: U.S. trade officials are undertaking a new review of a U.S.-Japan car trade pact that is likely to show disappointing results due to a strong dollar and lack of significant deregulation in Japan, industry officials said.

The report by the Clinton administration on the hard-fought 1995 trade agreement with Japan is scheduled to be released in mid-April and will likely show that many of the goals envisaged by U.S. industry and Clinton administration officials at the time the deal was signed have not been met.
"The situation in Japan is extraordinarily difficult," said Ford spokesman Al Chambers.

The Big Three U.S. automobile manufacturers -- Ford, Chrysler and General Motors -- had hoped to have at least 200 new dealers signed up in Japan to sell U.S.-brand cars by the end of 1996 and 1,000 new dealers by the year 2000.
As of last month, only about 114 dealers have been signed up, far short of the goal, according the the American Automobile Manufacturers Association.
The U.S. industry blames a weak yen against a strong dollar and a lack of significant deregulation to open up the car parts market for hurting U.S. efforts to sell more cars and parts in Japan.

The top corporate executives of the Big Three automakers had hoped to raise their concerns about the dollar and Japanese trade with President Clinton in a meeting that was scheduled for last week. But the meeting was postponed and the carmakers are trying to set a new date with the White House.

A disappointing report on the car trade agreement, which was reached in 1995 after long hours of negotiations under the shadow of U.S. trade sanctions against Japanese luxury cars, is likely to underscore the likelihood of fresh trade tensions between the two countries as the Japanese surplus rises.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told Japanese officials during a visit to Tokyo last week that a resurgence in the trade surplus would re-ignite frictions between the United States and Japan.

But at the same time he made some remarks that led currency traders to believe Washington still wanted a strong dollar. The U.S. currency has risen steadily since hitting its post-war low just under 80 yen two years ago.
"We don't believe in anybody using their currency for trade policies -- us or anybody else," Rubin said on Friday.

New data show the Japanese current account surplus, the broadest measure of trade, rising in February for the second month in a row. Monday's news of a widening of the surplus failed to dent bullish sentiment toward the dollar, which jumped to a 50-month high of 125 yen.

The strong dollar and weak yen make U.S. goods more costly and Japanese goods less expensive in the United States. U.S. carmakers have lost about 2.5 percentage points of domestic market share, while Japanese carmakers have gained nearly two percentage points so far this year.

Rubin and U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky have warned Japan not to try to export its way out of recession and said they do not expect to see an increase in the trade imbalance between the two countries.
But U.S. manufacturers, worried about losing market share to cheap Japanese goods, say warnings are not enough.
"Warning the Japanese is notoriously unreliable, because the Japanese do not take warnings that seriously," said Gordon Richards, an economist for the National Association of Manufacturers.
"The only thing the Japanese will take seriously is a major change in the exchange rate," he added. "When the yen went to about 85 to a dollar, the Japanese took that very seriously."
